title: Why Your Pores Still Look Large After Cleansing—and What Facials Can Actually Do

textData.text: You wash your face. You use your skincare. You look in the mirror—and your pores are still there.

Before you reach for a stronger scrub or another “pore-erasing” serum, here is something worth knowing: visible pores do not automatically mean your skin is dirty or clogged. Oil production, follicle size, and changes in the surrounding skin all influence how noticeable pores become.
If you've ever searched
“how to minimize large pores,” “how to get rid of clogged pores,” or “what facial is best for large pores,”
you're definitely not the only one.
Large, visible pores are one of the most common skin concerns we hear about during facials at
Matrix Massage & Bodywork in Salem, Wisconsin
, especially from clients coming from
Paddock Lake, Salem Lakes, Bristol, Twin Lakes and the surrounding Kenosha County area
And one of the biggest misconceptions we hear is:
“My pores still look big, so they must not be clean.”
Not necessarily.
New research is giving us a much better picture of what makes pores look larger—and it turns out that
oiliness, clogged pores, blackheads and enlarged pores are related, but they are not the same thing.
That matters because constantly scrubbing, extracting and drying out your skin may not solve the problem you're actually seeing.
At Matrix Massage & Bodywork, our approach to
customized facials in Salem, WI
, starts with understanding what your skin needs—not assuming every concern requires deeper cleansing or more exfoliation.
The goal is clearer-looking, smoother, more comfortable skin. Not convincing you that normal skin should look like a filter.
How to Minimize Large Pores: What Actually Works—and What Facials Can Do
Pore size is not simply a measure of how thoroughly you wash your face.

A dermatology review identified three important contributors to enlarged facial pores: increased oil production, reduced elasticity around the pore, and the size of the hair follicle. Acne and hormonal influences can also play a role. That means two people with similar-looking pores may need very different approaches.
One person may have actual congestion. Another may have relatively clear pores that look more noticeable because of the surrounding skin’s structure.
Cleaning out a pore and improving its appearance are related goals, but they are not the same thing.
What newer research tells us
A study published in
Scientific Reports
on September 24, 2026, compared skin samples with different combinations of oiliness, enlarged pores, and comedones—the plugs associated with blackheads and whiteheads.

Researchers found different patterns of gene activity associated with oil production, pore enlargement, and comedone formation. Pore enlargement was associated with immune activity and changes involving the skin’s supporting tissue, not simply oil production. This was exploratory research, not a trial of a facial or skincare product; several authors worked for a cosmetics company.
The useful takeaway is straightforward:
we should not treat every visible pore as a cleansing problem.
Are those dots on your nose really blackheads?
Not necessarily.
Some of the small, fairly uniform dots on the nose are
sebaceous filaments
. These are normal structures that help oil move through the follicle to the skin’s surface. Unlike blackheads, they are not plugs blocking the pore.
They can become more noticeable, but their presence does not mean your skin is unhealthy. And because they serve a normal function, removing their contents does not keep them empty permanently.
This is why we do not consider “extract every visible dot” a sensible facial goal. There is a difference between addressing congestion and repeatedly irritating normal skin.
Can a Facial Help Minimize Large Pores?
A more useful question is:
What is making my pores noticeable, and which parts can we improve?

The American Academy of Dermatology recommends approaches such as gentle cleansing, appropriate exfoliation, and managing clogged pores to make pores less noticeable. It also warns that scrubbing and squeezing can cause irritation that makes them look more prominent.

For a professional facial, that means focusing on appropriate cosmetic goals: addressing accessible congestion, refining surface texture, and keeping the skin comfortable—not promising to permanently erase pores.
Facials for Large Pores, Blackheads and Clogged Pores in Salem, WI
Our facial pathways help us organize treatment around the concern rather than give everyone the same protocol.
For visible congestion and excess surface oil,
Clear + Balance
may be the right direction.

This pathway can include cleansing, controlled exfoliation, steam only when tolerated, and targeted extractions followed by calming and hydrating care. The emphasis is on addressing appropriate, non-inflamed congestion—not working aggressively over irritated skin.
For tight, dry, or easily irritated skin, hydration or calming care may come first.
Hydrate + Restore
and
Calm + Support
allow us to prioritize comfort and moisture support rather than automatically adding stronger exfoliation.
For dullness and rough surface texture,
Brighten + Smooth
may be more appropriate.
The focus is controlled smoothing with hydration and barrier support, adjusted to what your skin can tolerate.
You do not need to arrive knowing which pathway to choose. That is part of the conversation.
What you use between facials matters, too
Our retail recommendations should make your routine easier to understand—not leave you with a shelf full of products you are unsure how to combine.
Before adding something new, we want to know what you already use, what feels comfortable, and what seems to make things worse.
Start with the right cleanser—not the strongest one
A cleanser should clean without making your routine an endurance test. Hot water and aggressive scrubbing can irritate skin; gentle cleansing is the better starting point.
In our home-care plans, a
Circadia cleanser
is selected according to the skin’s needs. A clarifying direction may suit some clients, while others need a gentler option.
The important question is not, “Which cleanser sounds the most powerful?”
It is, “Which cleanser fits my skin and the rest of my routine?”
Choose an active ingredient with a purpose

Salicylic acid can help unclog pores, while retinol may help some people with oily skin, mild acne, or reduced firmness. Neither is automatically right for every person. Retinol can irritate, and the AAD advises avoiding retinol products during pregnancy and breastfeeding.

More active ingredients do not automatically create better results. Using exfoliants alongside retinol, prescription retinoids, or other drying treatments can increase irritation. Your current products and skin response should guide how much exfoliation is appropriate.
Sometimes the most useful recommendation is not another serum. It is a clearer plan for the products you already have.
Do not confuse oil control with skipping moisture

Skin that feels oily can still need a moisturizer, particularly when acne products are causing dryness or irritation. The AAD recommends choosing a suitable non-comedogenic moisturizer and notes that moisturizing can improve tolerance of drying acne treatments.
For Matrix clients experiencing tightness or dehydration, our home-care guidance may include
Matrix Multi-Molecular Weight Hyaluronic Acid
, followed by an appropriate moisturizer.
We position it as hydration support—not as a product that permanently shrinks pores. Every product should have a clear job.
Keep sun protection in the routine
Daily sun protection belongs in a thoughtful skincare plan. The AAD recommends broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen with
SPF 30 or higher
, along with shade and protective clothing. Reapply according to the label, especially when outdoors, swimming, or sweating. Sun protection also helps prevent premature skin aging.
It may not be the most exciting step on your bathroom counter, but it deserves a consistent place there.
How often should you get a facial for clogged pores?
There is no single appointment schedule that fits everyone.

At Matrix, we consider the amount of congestion, skin sensitivity, your home-care routine, and how your skin responds before recommending the next visit. A short series with reassessment may make sense for recurring congestion; other clients need a less intensive maintenance approach.
We would rather adjust the plan than keep repeating a treatment simply because it is on the calendar.
Temporary redness can follow extractions. Persistent irritation is not a result we want you to push through.
When does a pore concern need more than a facial?
Painful, inflamed, open, or infected areas are not a reason to intensify extractions. Those concerns may need medical care rather than routine cosmetic treatment.
Acne can also require more than a cleanser or an exfoliant. When a concern is outside the scope of a facial, a dermatologist can evaluate it and discuss appropriate treatment.
Being thoughtful about that boundary is part of good skincare.
A clearer approach to facials in Salem, WI
At Matrix, we want you to understand both the treatment and the reason behind it.

That may mean focusing on congestion. It may mean reducing unnecessary exfoliation. It may mean selecting a cleanser and moisturizer that work more comfortably together instead of adding three more steps.
For busy people, a useful skincare plan needs to fit real life. You should know what you are using, why you are using it, and what kind of improvement is reasonable to expect.
The goal is not poreless skin. It is skin that looks clearer, feels better, and is supported by a routine you understand.
